channel.title: Liber Copia: Military History Podcast - WW2, Army, Navy and Air Force Films
channel.description: Military history from the original films. Each episode narrates a restored U.S. government film from World War II and the Cold War era (Army Air Forces mission reports, Navy and Army training films, War Department orientation films) against the film's own words, with quoted lines read in a second voice. Topics include the air war over Germany, naval and amphibious history, counterintelligence and secrecy discipline, combat psychiatry, and the logistics of war. Sources are public-domain films from the U.S. National Archives. The narration voice is synthetic; the archival film is unaltered. Keywords: military history, world war 2 history, history of war, war history, military tactics, intelligence analysis, field manual, espionage.
channel.itunes:author: Liber Copia LLC

item.title: Challenger: The Decision to Launch, from the Rogers Commission Report
item.description:
On January 28, 1986 it was 36 degrees Fahrenheit at launch, 15 degrees colder than any shuttle launch before it. The night before, engineers had tried to stop it. An original retelling of the decision to launch Challenger, built on the official report of the Rogers Commission (a U.S. government document in the public domain), with quoted lines marked. The narration voice is AI-generated.
An original podcast episode from Liber Copia.

item.description: How a division less than nine months old planned and carried out the amphibious assault at Oroku, Okinawa, in June 1945, told from the U.S. Marine Corps' own history of the campaign: The Final Campaign: Marines in the Victory on Okinawa, by Colonel Joseph H. item.title: Special Forces 1961: Fort Bragg to a bridge in the Alps
item.description:
The Big Picture was the U.S. Army's official report for the armed forces and the American people. This 1961 issue, introduced by Henry Fonda, follows the Special Forces from the Special Warfare Center at Fort Bragg to a training mission in the Alps: a parachute drop, a partisan camp, and a railway bridge with fifteen minutes left on the schedule.
Everything said here comes from the film's own narration. Lines quoted from the film are read in a second voice.
The narration voice is synthetic; the archival film is unaltered.
Source: The Big Picture: Special Forces (1961), U.S. Army, produced by the Army Pictorial Center. U.S. National Archives (gov.archives.arc.2569782), via the Internet Archive. Public domain: a work of the U.S. Government, with no copyright notice on the film.

item.title: The Army Occupied Walt Disney's Studio in 1941 — Here's What They Made
item.description:
On 8 December 1941, the day after Pearl Harbor, the United States Army moved into Walt Disney's studio in Burbank. They brought vehicles and ammunition and stayed about eight months - because the Lockheed aircraft plant was next door and the Army wanted anti-aircraft cover for it.
For the rest of the war most of what the studio produced was not entertainment. It was training films for the services and for war industry, health films for Latin America, and more than a thousand unit insignia designed free of charge. This one is Four Methods of Flush Riveting, made for the Lockheed Aircraft Corporation in 1942.
Why animate a rivet? Because a camera cannot see inside a sheet of metal and a drawing can. The film cuts through the join to show the metal deforming under the rivet head - something no photograph of a real riveting gun could show a trainee.
Three questions at the end, with the answers.
Source film: Four Methods of Flush Riveting (1942). Its own title cards carry no copyright notice, which places it in the public domain. Narration is read by a synthetic voice; the archival film is unaltered.
SOURCE When the Army Occupied Walt Disney's Studio (1941-45) — Walt Disney Studio for Lockheed Aircraft (source film); Liber Copia (edition) — 1942 https://archive.org/details/walt-disney-world-war-ii-propaganda-films
WHAT IS SAID IN THIS VIDEO On the eighth of December, nineteen forty-one, the day after Pearl Harbor, the United States Army moved into Walt Disney's studio in Burbank, California. Not for a tour. They brought vehicles and ammunition, and they stayed for about eight months. The reason was next door. The Lockheed aircraft plant was one of the most important factories in America, and the Army wanted anti-aircraft guns and men close to it. Disney's lot had the space. The studio that made Snow White spent the war explaining rivets. Full film on the channel.

item.title: When a Flare Goes Up, Close One Eye — US Army Field Manual FM 21-75
item.description:
An enemy flare blinds everyone who watches it, including the man who fired it. Close one eye while it burns and that eye still has its night vision when the light dies. It is one instruction out of a 1984 U.S. Army field manual, FM 21-75, Combat Skills of the Soldier — the book that tells an ordinary soldier how to stay alive.
Most of it is about being seen: movement draws the eye before colour or noise does; shine gives you away (a watch face, glasses, a lit cigarette); the human outline is the easiest shape for a human eye to recognise. A rush across open ground lasts three to five seconds, because that is less time than a machine gunner needs to track you. And when a position is camouflaged, the soldier walks 35 metres forward, turns, and judges his own work from where the enemy will be standing.
Three questions at the end, with the answers.
Illustrations are the manual's own figures. FM 21-75, Headquarters Department of the Army, 3 August 1984 — a work of the U.S. Government, public domain. The narration is read by a synthetic voice.
SOURCE How the U.S. Army teaches a soldier not to be seen (FM 21-75) — U.S. Department of the Army (source manual); Liber Copia (edition) — 1984 https://archive.org/details/milmanual-fm-21-75-combat-skills-of-the-soldier
WHAT IS SAID IN THIS VIDEO When an enemy flare goes up at night, it blinds everyone who looks at it. Including the man who fired it. So the U.S. Army's field manual tells a soldier to close one eye while it burns. When the light dies, that eye still has its night vision, and he can see while everyone around him cannot. It comes from FM 21-75, Combat Skills of the Soldier, and most of that book is about not being seen. Movement catches the eye before colour or noise does. Shine gives you away: a watch, a ring, a wet mess tin. And your outline is the thing a human being recognises fastest of all, so you break it up. Then the rule that holds the rest together. Judge your own position from where the enemy is standing, not from where you are.

item.title: The USS Forrestal Fire: The Navy Filmed Its Own Worst Day
item.description:
On 29 July 1967 the aircraft carrier USS Forrestal was at Yankee Station off Vietnam, out of range of any hostile fire. A Zuni rocket fired by itself across the flight deck and hit a parked A-4 Skyhawk. Two 1,000-pound bombs fell from its wings into burning fuel. Nine major explosions went off in the first five minutes. 134 men were killed or listed as missing.
Almost all of it was recorded by the ship's own PLAT camera - a television camera on the island that watched the flight deck through every launch, taped so crews could be debriefed afterwards. It was still running.
What makes the Navy's 1973 film about that tape remarkable is that it does not defend anyone. It stops the footage and names what it sees: fuelling under way while ordnance was still being armed, bombs being strong-backed into place by hand instead of hoisted, men out of uniform and out of position, fog foam stations that had never been charged, and water hose teams washing away the foam that was working. "Leadership and on-deck communications," it says, "were early casualties of the Forrestal fire."
Then it showed that film to the fleet, and rebuilt shipboard firefighting training around it.
SOURCE The Navy Filmed Its Own Worst Day at Sea — Naval Photographic Center, U.S. Navy — 1973 https://archive.org/details/gov.ntis.ava19833vnb1
WHAT IS SAID IN THIS VIDEO In 1967 a rocket fired by itself across the flight deck of the carrier USS Forrestal. The ship's own bridge camera was taping at the time, and it caught all of it. When the Navy cut that tape into a training film six years later, it did not defend anybody. It pointed at the fuelling going on while ordnance was still being armed. At men moving thousand-pound bombs by hand. At fog foam stations that had never been charged. And it wrote this about itself. Leadership and on-deck communications were early casualties of the Forrestal fire. A hundred and thirty-four men were killed. The Navy showed the film to the fleet and rebuilt its firefighting training around it. The last card in the film is two words. Learn or burn.

item.title: They Flew 12,650 Warplanes — and the Army Wouldn't Send Their Bodies Home (WASP, 1944)
item.description:
When WASP pilot Mabel Rawlinson died in a burning trainer at Camp Davis in 1944, the Army would not pay to send her body home. The other pilots put the money together themselves.
The Women Airforce Service Pilots flew for the United States Army Air Forces between 1942 and 1944, but on paper they were civilians. 25,000 applied; 1,074 qualified. They ferried 12,650 aircraft of 78 types from the factories to the airfields, and towed canvas targets while gunners on the ground fired live anti-aircraft rounds. Thirty-eight were killed. There was no insurance, no flag on the coffin.
The programme was disbanded in December 1944, eight months before the war ended, and the records were sealed for 33 years. Veteran status came only in 1977; the Congressional Gold Medal in 2009.
Photographs: U.S. National Archives and the Library of Congress, public domain. The narration is read by a synthetic voice; the photographs are unaltered.
SOURCE WASP: 12,650 aircraft, 38 dead, 33 years sealed — Liber Copia (images: U.S. National Archives, Library of Congress) — 2026 https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Women_Airforce_Service_Pilots
WHAT IS SAID IN THIS VIDEO In 1944 a pilot named Mabel Rawlinson died in a burning trainer at Camp Davis, North Carolina. The Army would not pay to send her body home. The other women pilots put the money together themselves. They were the Women Airforce Service Pilots. Twenty-five thousand applied. One thousand and seventy-four qualified. They ferried twelve thousand six hundred and fifty aircraft, of seventy-eight different types, from the factories to the airfields. They towed targets while gunners on the ground fired live ammunition at the sleeve behind them. Thirty-eight of them were killed. On paper they were civilians, so there was no flag for the coffin and no gold star for the family. The programme was disbanded in December 1944. Its records were sealed and classified for thirty-three years, which is why you were never taught this.

item.title: "They Never Lost a Bomber" — The Tuskegee Airmen Myth, and the Better Truth
item.description:
For fifty years one sentence followed the Tuskegee Airmen: they never lost a bomber they escorted. It was printed in newspapers, spoken at ceremonies and built into a film. It is not true — and the real record is more impressive than the legend.
In 2007 Air Force historian Daniel Haulman went through the mission reports of the 332nd Fighter Group. On 179 bomber escort missions, at least 27 bombers under their protection were shot down. The other escort groups of the Fifteenth Air Force lost far more.
This film covers the 1925 Army War College study that shaped Army policy, Benjamin O. Davis Jr.'s four silent years at West Point, the 1943 report that nearly removed the 99th Fighter Squadron from combat, the record the 332nd actually left, the 101 officers arrested at Freeman Field in 1945, and Executive Order 9981.
Photographs: U.S. National Archives and the Library of Congress, all public domain. Narration is read by a synthetic voice; the photographs are unaltered.
Sources: Daniel L. Haulman, Air Force Historical Research Agency (2007); National Archives photographs by Toni Frissell, March 1945.
SOURCE The Tuskegee Airmen bomber-loss myth — Liber Copia (images: U.S. National Archives, Library of Congress) — 2026 https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Tuskegee_Airmen

item.title: Target for Today: one 1944 bombing mission, start to finish
item.description:
Target for Today is a 1944 Army Air Forces film, made by the First Motion Picture Unit, that follows one Eighth Air Force mission from start to finish: the weather room, the planning, the ground crews working through the night, the three o'clock wake-up, the briefings, the bomb run, and the count as the planes come home.
Everything said here comes from the film's own narration and dialogue. Lines quoted from the film are read in a second voice.
The narration is a synthetic (AI-generated) voice. The footage is the original film, unaltered apart from scaling; the film's original soundtrack is not used.
Source: Target for Today (1944), First Motion Picture Unit, Army Air Forces, U.S. War Department. Internet Archive, NTIS AVA11757VNB1. Public domain: a work of the U.S. Government, with no copyright notice on the film's cards.

item.title: The Machinery Behind Ike and Winston
item.description:
Today we are asking a question that a photograph cannot answer: how do allies turn agreement about an enemy into agreement about an operation? Churchill and Eisenhower offer a useful case because their names invite a personal explanation. One was an experienced political leader, the other an American officer who became a coalition commander. It is tempting to say that friendship connected them and victory followed. But that leaves out the difficult middle. Someone still had to decide where forces would go, what resources they would receive, and whose decisions would be binding. Our subject is that middle: the machinery that allowed a partnership to survive disagreement.
Original history programme for Liber Copia. Independently researched; not an adaptation or reading of Jonathan W. Jordan’s book.

item.title: Old Friends in a Nuclear World
item.description:
Today's question is what happens when an old partnership enters a world it was not originally built to manage. Churchill and Eisenhower had worked together in the defeat of Nazi Germany. By nineteen fifty-three, Eisenhower was president of the United States and Churchill was serving a second term as Britain's prime minister. They could draw on wartime familiarity, but the problems before them had changed. Nuclear weapons and the Cold War made the consequences of disagreement very different. We will examine their relationship through offices, evidence and chronology, without assuming that friendship either controlled every decision or meant nothing at all.
Original history programme for Liber Copia. Independently researched; not an adaptation or reading of Jonathan W. Jordan’s book.

item.title: D-Day and the Burden of Uncertainty
item.description:
Think about a decision whose success cannot be known when it has to be made. That is the problem at the centre of today's episode. We are looking at the preparations for D-Day through the relationship between Churchill and Eisenhower, but our main subject is uncertainty. Histories of command often end with a confident order and then move directly to the result. Between those two moments lie risks that no speech or signature could remove. The evidence of June nineteen forty-four is valuable because it lets us distinguish three things: confidence expressed to an army, information available to a commander, and responsibility for what might happen next.
Original history programme for Liber Copia. Independently researched; not an adaptation or reading of Jonathan W. Jordan’s book.
